For while we live we are always being given up to death for
Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our
mortal flesh." And in these verses there is another thing to be
observed: all that Paul has previously named, affliction and
perplexity, persecution and assault, is now included under
one heading: "Always carrying in the body the death of
Jesus." That is to say that he understands all our sufferings
in the light of the cross. For Paul the cross of Christ is not
simply an historical event belonging to a remote past, but an
event which, initiated in Christ, penetrates the whole of
human history; it is the event in which God pronounces this
whole world here below, with all its pride and pageantry,
all its cruel distress and pain, to be as nothing. This dying
of Christ is repeated wherever a man understands that his
suffering is meant to serve the purpose of reminding him
that this present world is provisional only and ultimately
doomed to destruction. And the resurrection life of Christ is
actualized wherever man takes up the cross of Christ, which
means that he refuses to cling to this-worldly realities, that
he lets them slide in order that God may bestow upon him
the life of the transcendent world of the spirit.
Hence all our suffering is meant to cause us to become in-
wardly released from the fascination of the this-worldly and
the visible, to become wholly abandoned to the self-bestow-
ing grace of God-that grace which wills to confer upon us
true eternal life. This is the life of which we can have no
conception; for we can conceive only a life according to the
realities of this world. Nevertheless we are permitted to
glimpse something of that higher life just because we live
here in two worlds, because, while through the body we are
involved in the visible, we may raise our hearts and minds to
the world of the spirit and of grace. "But we have this
treasure in earthen vessels, to show that the transcendent
power belongs to God and not to us." What so often appears
to us as a torment, indeed as a curse, namely, the fact that
we live in two worlds, is in truth a grace; for by it we learn
